claim: Immobilization decreases the number of PAX7+ muscle progenitors by 58.07% (±17.66) in paralyzed compared to control muscles.
source: Two days after the inhibition of muscle contraction, we observed a reduction in the overall muscle size (Figure 1D,H), which is consistent with previous reports (Crow and Stockdale, 1986; Hall and Herring, 1990). In addition, we observed a decrease of 58.07% (±17.66) in the number of PAX7+ muscle progenitors in paralyzed compared to control muscles (Figure 1B,D-F,H-J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from immunohistochemistry experiments shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: The relative expression levels of PAX7 and MYF5 genes are significantly decreased in DMB-treated limbs compared to control limbs as early as 12 hr after DMB application.
source: Consistently, the relative expression levels of PAX7 and MYF5 genes were significantly decreased in DMB-treated limbs compared to control limbs, as early as 12 hr after DMB application and with a more prominent effect at 48 hr (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Immobilization increases myogenic differentiation assessed by increased MYOD and MYOG expression.
source: In addition to the reduction of the muscle progenitor pool, we also observed an increase of myogenic differentiation assessed by an increase of MYOD and MYOG expression using RT-q-PCR or in situ hybridization in immobilized limbs compared to control limbs (Figure 1C,G,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Muscle fibers are larger in limb muscles of DMB-treated fetuses compared to control muscles.
source: In addition, muscle fibers were larger in limb muscles of DMB-treated fetuses compared to control muscles (Figure 1E,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 1.

claim: Large muscle fibers in paralyzed muscles are associated with several nuclei, while control muscle fibers display only one nucleus on transverse sections.
source: The large muscle fibers were associated with several nuclei in paralyzed muscles, while control muscle fibers displayed only one nucleus on transverse sections (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Pancuronium bromide (PB) treatment leads to a 28.92% (±7.27) reduction in the number of PAX7+ cells.
source: Injection of pancuronium bromide (PB), a drug that exerts a flaccid skeletal muscle paralysis (Nowlan et al., 2010) led to a similar but less pronounced effect, i.e. a 28.92% (±7.27) reduction in the number of PAX7+ cells and a concomitant increase of muscle differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: DMB or PB treatments of chick fetal myoblast cultures do not affect muscle progenitors or their differentiation.
source: DMB or PB treatments of chick fetal myoblast cultures did neither affect muscle progenitors nor their differentiation and did not change the expression levels of PAX7, MYF5, MYOD and MYOG (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that DMB and PB did not have any off-target effect on myogenic cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro culture experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inhibition of muscle contraction leading to rigid or flaccid paralysis reduces the pool of fetal muscle progenitors and increases their propensity to differentiate.
source: We conclude that the inhibition of muscle contraction leading to rigid or flaccid paralysis reduces the pool of fetal muscle progenitors and increases their propensity to differentiate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1 supplements.

claim: During fetal myogenesis, the NOTCH ligand JAG2 is expressed in MF20+ differentiated muscle cells.
source: During fetal myogenesis, the NOTCH ligand JAG2 was expressed in MF20+ differentiated muscle cells (Delfini et al. 2000), while HES5 a recognized transcriptional readout of NOTCH activity (Andersson et al., 2011) was excluded from differentiated muscle fibers (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2 and cited literature.

claim: HES5, a transcriptional readout of NOTCH activity, is excluded from differentiated muscle fibers.
source: During fetal myogenesis, the NOTCH ligand JAG2 was expressed in MF20+ differentiated muscle cells (Delfini et al. 2000), while HES5 a recognized transcriptional readout of NOTCH activity (Andersson et al., 2011) was excluded from differentiated muscle fibers (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2 and cited literature.

claim: JAG2 and HES5 expression is decreased in paralyzed muscles compared to control muscles.
source: In immobilized fetuses, the expression of the JAG2 and HES5 was decreased in paralyzed muscles (Figure 2C,F,I) compared to control muscles (Figure 2B,E,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: JAG2 and HES5 expression in blood vessels is not affected in paralyzed muscles.
source: We believe that the downregulation of JAG2 and HES5 expression in paralyzed muscles reflected a muscle-specific loss of gene expression, since JAG2 and HES5 expression was not affected in blood vessels (Figure 2B,C,E,F,H,I, arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: JAG2 and HES5 mRNA levels are moderately but significantly downregulated in limbs of immobilized animals.
source: Consistently, the JAG2 and HES5 mRNA levels were moderately but significantly downregulated in limbs of immobilized animals (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: HEYL mRNA levels are significantly downregulated in limbs of immobilized animals compared to controls.
source: The relative mRNA levels of HEYL gene were also significantly downregulated in limbs of immobilized animals compared to controls (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: NOTCH activity is reduced in paralyzed muscles.
source: In summary, NOTCH activity was reduced in paralyzed muscles, as assessed by reduced expression of the NOTCH ligand JAG2 in muscle fibers and of the transcriptional readout of NOTCH activity, HES5, in muscles.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Immobilization mimics a NOTCH loss-of-function phenotype in muscles.
source: The downregulation of NOTCH signaling (Figure 2) and the concomitant reduction of the muscle progenitor pool and increase of differentiation (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) observed in unloading conditions led us to conclude that immobilization mimics a NOTCH loss-of-function phenotype in muscles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: EdU incorporation into PAX7+ cells is not altered during immobilization compared to control conditions.
source: EdU incorporation into PAX7+ cells was not altered, indicating that the proliferative rate of PAX7+ cells was not changed during immobilization compared to control conditions (Figure 3A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: An increase of apoptotic figures is observed in fetal muscles of immobilized animals 48 hr after DMB treatment.
source: While apoptotic cells were very rare in control muscles (Figure 3H,J,L,N), we observed an increase of apoptotic figures in fetal muscles of immobilized animals, 48 hr after DMB treatment (Figure 3I,K,M,O).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Apoptotic figures are not observed in PAX7+ cells 48 hr after DMB treatments.
source: The apoptotic figures were not observed in PAX7+ cells, 48 hr after DMB treatments (Figure 3H–K), nor in MF20+ cells or in Desmin+ cells (Figure 3J–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Immobilization does not affect the proliferative capacity or apoptosis of PAX7+ cells.
source: Thus, immobilization did neither affect the proliferative capacity nor apoptosis of PAX7+ cells, which was reminiscent of the unchanged proliferation and apoptosis rate of muscle progenitors in NOTCH loss-of-function in mice (Vasuytina et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 3 and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Ligand-dependent NOTCH activation maintains the pool of PAX7+ cells at E9.5 despite inhibition of muscle differentiation.
source: In DLL1-activated NOTCH limbs, the pool of PAX7+ cells was maintained at E9.5, despite inhibition of muscle differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with the maintenance of PAX7+ progenitors in NICD-expressing cells in mouse fetuses (Mourikis et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and cited literature.

claim: In DLL1-expressing regions of immobilized limbs, the number of PAX7+ cells is increased by 215.81% (± 29.36) compared to control limbs.
source: In contrast, in DLL1-expressing regions of (right) limbs, the number of PAX7+ cells was increased by 215.81% (± 29.36) and myosin expression was decreased compared to control (left) limbs (Figure 4A–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Retroviral DELTA1-induced NOTCH rescues around 93% of the number of PAX7+ cells in paralyzed muscles.
source: Since immobilization leads to a 2.3-fold (58.07%) reduction in the number of PAX7+ cells (Figure 1B), we estimated that retroviral DELTA1-induced NOTCH rescued around 93% the number of PAX7+ cells in paralyzed muscles.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the data from Figures 1 and 4.

claim: NOTCH activation prevents the decrease in the number of PAX7+ cells by preventing their inappropriate differentiation under immobilization conditions.
source: We conclude that NOTCH activation prevents the decrease in the number of PAX7+ cells by preventing their inappropriate differentiation under immobilization conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NOTCH rescue experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The lack of NOTCH ligand activity in around 45% of differentiated muscle cells significantly decreases the number of PAX7+ cells by 32.42% (±7.23).
source: We observed that the lack of ligand activity in around 45% of differentiated muscle cells significantly decreased the number of PAX7+ cells by 32.42% (±7.23) compared to contralateral limbs (Figure 5F–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from dominant-negative DELTA1 experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: NOTCH ligand activity in muscle fibers is required to maintain the pool of fetal muscle progenitors.
source: We conclude that NOTCH ligand activity in muscle fibers is required to maintain the pool of fetal muscle progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dominant-negative DELTA1 experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: 89.6% (±3.65) of myonuclei of post-mitotic MF20+ cells display nuclear YAP protein.
source: Unexpectedly, given the proliferative role of YAP in organ formation and tumorigenesis (Zanconato et al. 2015, Piccolo et al., 2014), we found that 89.6% (±3.65) of myonuclei of post-mitotic MF20+ cells displayed nuclear YAP protein (Figure 6A-C,G,H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6 and cited literature.

claim: YAP nuclear staining is stronger than YAP cytoplasmic staining in MF20+ cells.
source: Moreover, YAP nuclear staining was stronger than YAP cytoplasmic staining in MF20+ cells; the cytoplasmic domains being delineated with MF20 staining (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 6.

claim: ANKRD1 and CTGF expression is observed at the tips of MF20+ muscle fibers.
source: ANKRD1 and CTGF expression was observed at the tips of MF20+ muscle fibers (Figure 6I-M,Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6.

claim: ANKRD1 is exclusively expressed in muscle fibers in fetal limbs.
source: In fetal limbs, ANKRD1 was exclusively expressed in muscle fibers (Figure 6I,K,L), whereas CTGF transcripts were observed also in cartilage (Figure 6M,Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6.

claim: ANKRD1 and CTGF expression is lost in muscle fibers of immobilized fetuses.
source: In immobilized fetuses, ANKRD1 and CTGF expression was lost in muscle fibers (Figure 6I–R), but CTGF expression was maintained in cartilage (Figure 6M,P–R).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6.

claim: ANKRD1 mRNA levels show a drastic diminution in immobilization conditions.
source: Consistently, the mRNA levels of ANKDR1 showed a drastic diminution, while those of CTGF displayed a significant but less strong reduction in immobilization conditions (Figure 6S).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR data shown in Figure 6S.

claim: CYR61 mRNA levels are decreased in limbs 48 hr after DMB treatment.
source: CYR61 mRNA levels were also decreased in limbs 48 hr after DMB treatment (Figure 6S).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR data shown in Figure 6S.

claim: The number of YAP+ myonuclei is significantly decreased in muscle fibers of paralyzed muscles compared to control muscles (dropping from 89.6% ± 3.66 to 15.9% ± 4.36).
source: Moreover, the number of YAP+ myonuclei was significantly decreased in muscle fibers of paralyzed muscles compared to control muscles (dropping from 89.6% ± 3.66 to 15.9% ± 4.36) (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: YAP activity is observed in muscle fibers of contracting muscles and this activity is lost in paralyzed muscles.
source: We conclude that YAP activity is observed in muscle fibers of contracting muscles and that this activity is lost in paralyzed muscles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the YAP localization and target gene expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: YapS112A activates YAP target gene expression (CTGF and CYR61) in fetal myoblasts.
source: Transfection of YapS112A/RCAS into fetal myoblasts increased the expression levels of YAP target genes (CTGF and CYR61) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR data from cell culture experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: YapS112A increases PAX7 and MYF5 expression and reduces MYOD and MYOG expression in fetal myoblasts.
source: In addition, we also observed changes in muscle gene expression, previously described in C2C12 cells and satellite cell-derived myoblasts (Judson et al., 2012; Watt et al., 2010), i.e. concomitant increase of PAX7 and MYF5 and reduction of MYOD and MYOG expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR data and cited literature.

claim: YapS112A activates JAG2 expression in fetal muscle cells.
source: YapS112A also activated JAG2 expression and NOTCH target genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: JAG2 expression is upregulated in differentiated muscle cells after transfection with MLC-Tomato-YapS112A.
source: JAG2 expression was also upregulated in differentiated muscle cells after transfection with MLC-Tomato-YapS112A (Tomato+ FACS-sorted cells) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-q-PCR data from FACS-sorted cells shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: YAP forced-activity in differentiated muscle cells activates ANKRD1 expression in paralyzed muscles.
source: We observed that YAP forced-activity in differentiated muscle cells activated ANKRD1 expression in paralyzed muscles compared to the loss of ANKRD1 in paralyzed muscles (Figure 7A,B,D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7.

claim: YAP forced-activity rescues JAG2 expression in paralyzed muscles.
source: YAP forced-activity also rescued JAG2 expression in paralyzed muscles compared to the loss of JAG2 in paralyzed muscles (Figure 7A,C,D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The number of PAX7+ cells is increased by 55.19% (± 10.2) in muscles displaying YapS112A expression in differentiated muscle cells compared to contralateral limbs.
source: Moreover, the number of PAX7+ cells was increased of 55.19% (± 10.2) in muscles displaying YapS112A expression in differentiated muscle cells (visualized with Tomato expression) compared to muscles of contralateral limbs (Figure 7G–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: YAP forced-activity in muscle fibers prevents the loss of JAG2 expression in muscle fibers and the decrease in the number of adjacent muscle progenitors in immobilization conditions.
source: We conclude that YAP forced-activity in muscle fibers prevents the loss of JAG2 expression in muscle fibers and the decrease in the number of adjacent muscle progenitors in immobilization conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the YAP rescue experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: YAP is recruited to a regulatory region (−629 bp; −1023 bp) in the JAG2 promoter that contains a MCAT element.
source: We identified a putative regulatory region (−629 bp; −1023 bp) in the JAG2 promoter, which contained a MCAT element (CATTCC), the known binding motif for TEAD complexes (Davidson et al., 1988). We found that YAP was recruited to this regulatory region based on PCR (Figure 8B) and RT-q-PCR (Figure 8D) analyses.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 8 and cited literature.

claim: YAP occupancy to the JAG2 promoter region is decreased in immobilized fetuses.
source: The YAP occupancy to this region was decreased in immobilized fetuses based on PCR (Figure 8C) and RT-q-PCR (Figure 8D) analyses, consistent with the decrease of JAG2 expression in muscle fibers in immobilization conditions (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Muscle contraction maintains the PAX7+ muscle progenitor pool during fetal myogenesis by preventing differentiation rather than affecting cell proliferation.
source: We show here that mechanical signals are required to maintain the PAX7+ muscle progenitor pool during fetal myogenesis. However, muscle contraction does not change cell proliferation but rather affects the maintenance of PAX7+ cells by preventing their differentiation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: NOTCH signaling acts downstream of mechanical signals during fetal myogenesis.
source: We provide evidence that NOTCH signaling emerges as a molecular pathway that acts downstream of mechanical forces to regulate the pool of muscle progenitors during development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NOTCH rescue experiments and immobilization studies.

claim: YAP acts on muscle progenitors in a NOTCH-dependent and non-cell autonomous manner during fetal myogenesis.
source: Using muscle unloading during fetal myogenesis, we provide evidence that YAP acts on muscle progenitors in a NOTCH–dependent and non-cell autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the YAP and NOTCH experiments showing YAP regulates JAG2 in fibers which affects progenitors.

claim: YAP positively regulates the expression of the NOTCH ligand JAG2 in muscle fibers upon muscle contraction.
source: Our results identify a novel mechanism acting downstream of muscle contraction, where YAP activates JAG2 expression in muscle fibers, which in turn regulates the pool of fetal muscle progenitors via NOTCH in a non-cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including ChIP, rescue experiments, and expression analyses.

claim: Loss of NOTCH signaling results in a reduction of the progenitor pool due to premature muscle differentiation in mice.
source: NOTCH loss-of-function experiments in mice induce a loss of the muscle progenitor pool due to premature muscle differentiation (Bröhl et al., 2012; Czajkowski et al., 2014; Schuster-Gossler et al., 2007; Vasyutina et al., 2007), whereas NOTCH activation represses muscle differentiation in chick and mouse embryos (Delfini et al., 2000; Hirsinger et al., 2001; Mourikis et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing NOTCH loss-of-function experiments in mice.

claim: NOTCH activation represses muscle differentiation in chick and mouse embryos.
source: NOTCH loss-of-function experiments in mice induce a loss of the muscle progenitor pool due to premature muscle differentiation (Bröhl et al., 2012; Czajkowski et al., 2014; Schuster-Gossler et al., 2007; Vasyutina et al., 2007), whereas NOTCH activation represses muscle differentiation in chick and mouse embryos (Delfini et al., 2000; Hirsinger et al., 2001; Mourikis et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing NOTCH activation experiments.

claim: YAP promotes satellite cell proliferation and inhibits muscle differentiation in culture.
source: Similarly to NOTCH, the co-transcriptional activator YAP (Yes-Associated Protein) promotes satellite cell proliferation and inhibits muscle differentiation in culture (Judson et al., 2012; Watt et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP function in cultured satellite cells.

claim: YAP has been identified as a sensor of mechanical activity and mediates cellular and transcriptional responses downstream of mechanical forces.
source: In addition to being a nuclear effector of the Hippo pathway, YAP has been identified as a sensor of mechanical activity and mediates cellular and transcriptional responses downstream of mechanical forces (Aragona et al., 2013; Dupont et al., 2011; Porazinski et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP as a mechanosensor.

claim: YAP and TEAD1 occupy 80% of the same promoters in human mammary epithelial cells.
source: YAP and TEAD1 have been shown to occupy 80% of the same promoters in human mammary epithelial cells (Zhao et al., 2008), indicating that YAP/TEAD interaction could constitute the major molecular mechanism of YAP-mediated regulation of gene transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP and TEAD1 co-occupancy of promoters.

claim: YAP is a critical regulator of skeletal muscle fiber size in adult mice.
source: In addition to being involved in muscle stem cell proliferation (Judson et al., 2012; Watt et al., 2010), YAP has been recently shown to be a critical regulator of skeletal muscle fiber size in adult mice (Goodman et al., 2015; Watt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP function in adult muscle fiber size regulation.

claim: Fetal myogenesis depends on PAX7-expressing muscle progenitors and is associated with muscle growth.
source: Fetal myogenesis depends on PAX7-expressing muscle progenitors and is associated with muscle growth (Hutcheson et al., 2009; Kassar-Duchossoy, 2005; Relaix et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing fetal myogenesis.

claim: By the end of fetal myogenesis, PAX7+ cells adopt a satellite cell position under the basal lamina of muscle fibers.
source: By the end of fetal myogenesis, PAX7+ cells adopt a satellite cell position under the basal lamina of muscle fibers (Biressi et al., 2007; Bröhl et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing PAX7+ cell positioning.

claim: Mechanical forces generated by muscle contraction are essential for the correct establishment of the musculoskeletal system during development.
source: During development, mechanical forces generated by muscle contraction are essential for the correct establishment of the musculoskeletal system.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the context of the introduction and cited literature.

claim: The influence of mechanical forces for cartilage, joint, and bone development has been previously addressed.
source: Although the influence of the mechanical forces for cartilage, joint, and bone development has been previously addressed (Nowlan et al., 2010; Rolfe et al., 2014; Shwartz et al., 2013), the consequence of muscle-induced mechanical load for the development of muscle itself is largely unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing mechanical forces in skeletal development.

claim: The consequence of muscle-induced mechanical load for the development of muscle itself is largely unknown.
source: Although the influence of the mechanical forces for cartilage, joint, and bone development has been previously addressed (Nowlan et al., 2010; Rolfe et al., 2014; Shwartz et al., 2013), the consequence of muscle-induced mechanical load for the development of muscle itself is largely unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Activation of the NOTCH signaling pathway requires direct cell-cell contact between a signal-sending cell that expresses the NOTCH ligand and a signal-receiving cell that expresses the NOTCH receptor.
source: Activation of the NOTCH signaling pathway requires direct cell-cell contact between a signal-sending cell that expresses the NOTCH ligand and a signal-receiving cell that expresses the NOTCH receptor.
evidence: This is a description of the NOTCH signaling mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: Upon ligand activation, the intracellular domain of the NOTCH receptor is cleaved, translocates into the nucleus, associates with the transcription factor RBPJ and activates the transcription of HES and HEY genes.
source: Upon ligand activation, the intracellular domain of the NOTCH receptor is cleaved, translocates into the nucleus, associates with the transcription factor RBPJ and activates the transcription of the bHLH transcriptional repressor genes, HES and HEY [reviewed in Andersson et al. (2011)].
evidence: The claim describes the NOTCH signaling mechanism based on cited review.

claim: In adult myogenesis, NOTCH is involved in satellite cell activation, proliferation and quiescence.
source: In adult myogenesis, NOTCH is involved in satellite cell activation, proliferation and quiescence [reviewed in Mourikis and Tajbakhsh (2014)] and the absence of NOTCH signaling in muscle stem cells results in satellite cell depletion due to premature differentiation (Bjornson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing NOTCH function in adult myogenesis.

claim: The absence of NOTCH signaling in muscle stem cells results in satellite cell depletion due to premature differentiation.
source: In adult myogenesis, NOTCH is involved in satellite cell activation, proliferation and quiescence [reviewed in Mourikis and Tajbakhsh (2014)] and the absence of NOTCH signaling in muscle stem cells results in satellite cell depletion due to premature differentiation (Bjornson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing NOTCH loss-of-function in adult muscle stem cells.

claim: During developmental myogenesis, active NOTCH signaling is associated with proliferating muscle progenitors, while NOTCH ligands are expressed in differentiated muscle cells.
source: During developmental myogenesis, active NOTCH signaling is associated with proliferating muscle progenitors, while NOTCH ligands are expressed in differentiated muscle cells (Delfini et al., 2000; Vasyutina et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing NOTCH expression patterns during development.

claim: NOTCH has been described to activate embryonic myogenesis in somites.
source: In addition, during development, NOTCH has been described to activate embryonic myogenesis in somites (Rios et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing NOTCH function in somites.

claim: Upstream regulators of NOTCH signaling during developmental myogenesis have not attracted attention.
source: While studies have identified NOTCH target genes in fetal muscle progenitors (Bröhl et al., 2012; Mourikis et al., 2012), upstream regulators of NOTCH signaling during developmental myogenesis have not attracted attention.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The subcellular localization of YAP protein reflects its transcriptional activity.
source: Since the subcellular localization of YAP protein reflects its transcriptional activity (Dupont et al., 2011), we examined nuclear YAP staining in MF20+ and PAX7+ cells.
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP localization and activity.

claim: ANKRD1 is a muscle ankyrin-repeat protein that binds sarcomeric proteins.
source: ANKRD1 is a muscle ankyrin-repeat protein that binds sarcomeric proteins (Kojic et al., 2011), and CTGF is a secreted matricellular protein involved in multiple cellular processes (Malik et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing ANKRD1 function.

claim: CTGF is a secreted matricellular protein involved in multiple cellular processes.
source: ANKRD1 is a muscle ankyrin-repeat protein that binds sarcomeric proteins (Kojic et al., 2011), and CTGF is a secreted matricellular protein involved in multiple cellular processes (Malik et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing CTGF function.

claim: ANKRD1 and CTGF are recognized direct target genes of YAP in many cell types.
source: ANKRD1 and CTGF are two recognized direct target genes of YAP in many cell types (Lai et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP target genes.

claim: CYR61 is a matricellular protein of the same family as CTGF and is also a YAP target gene.
source: CYR61 is another matricellular protein of the same family as CTGF and is also a YAP target gene (Lai et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing CYR61 as a YAP target.

claim: TEAD transcription factors recognize and bind to MCAT elements (CATTCC), which are enriched in regulatory regions of muscle-related genes.
source: The TEAD transcription factors recognize and bind to MCAT elements (CATTCC), which are enriched in regulatory regions of muscle-related genes [reviewed in Wackerhage et al. (2014)].
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing TEAD binding motifs.

claim: Oncogenic YAP variants activate the NOTCH ligand JAG1 and consequently NOTCH signaling in hepatocellular carcinoma cells.
source: Oncogenic YAP variants activate the NOTCH ligand JAG1 and consequently NOTCH signaling in hepatocellular carcinoma cells (Tschaharganeh et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP-NOTCH interactions in cancer.

claim: TEAD binds to regulatory sequences of the JAG1 gene in human breast cancer cells.
source: Moreover, TEAD binds to regulatory sequences of the JAG1 gene in human breast cancer cells (Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing TEAD binding to JAG1.

claim: YAP and NOTCH pathways converge to promote proliferation, cell fate and differentiation in a cell-autonomous manner in vertebrates.
source: The current view is that YAP and NOTCH pathways converge to promote proliferation, cell fate and differentiation in a cell-autonomous manner in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a summary of the current understanding in the field based on the literature.

claim: Yorkie (Drosophila YAP equivalent) activates Serrate to induce responses in neighboring cells during crystal cell differentiation in hematopoiesis.
source: This mechanism is reminiscent of that of the Drosophila YAP equivalent, Yorkie, during crystal cell differentiation in hematopoiesis, where Yorkie activates Serrate to induce responses in neighboring cells (Ferguson and Martinez-Agosto, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing Yorkie function in Drosophila.

claim: Mechanical forces exerted by the signal-sending cell are required for ligand-induced NOTCH activation in a receiving cell.
source: Interestingly, on a molecular level, mechanical forces exerted by the signal-sending cell are required for ligand-induced NOTCH activation in a receiving cell that does not appear to sense forces directly (Gordon et al., 2015; Wang and Ha, 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing mechanical requirements for NOTCH activation.

claim: The NOTCH ligand Jagged1 rescues the Duchenne muscular dystrophy phenotype in zebrafish embryos.
source: Lastly, the NOTCH ligand Jagged1 rescues the Duchenne muscular dystrophy phenotype in zebrafish embryos and is upregulated in mildly affected dystrophin-deficient dogs (Vieira et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing Jagged1 function in muscular dystrophy models.

claim: Swimming-induced exercises lead to extensive transcriptional changes in fast muscles in zebrafish, including modification of the expression of NOTCH ligands Dll1, Jag1 and Jag2.
source: In zebrafish, swimming-induced exercises lead to extensive transcriptional changes in fast muscles, including modification of the expression of NOTCH ligands, Dll1, Jag1 and Jag2 in addition to other NOTCH components (Palstra et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing exercise effects on NOTCH ligands in zebrafish.

claim: NOTCH components are downregulated in bones of muscleless limbs of Spd mutant mice.
source: NOTCH components are also downregulated in bones of muscleless limbs of Spd mutant mice (Rolfe et al., 2014), although there is no described NOTCH loss-of-function phenotype in bones of muscleless limbs or immobilized embryos.
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing NOTCH expression in muscleless limbs.

claim: The NOTCH pathway has been proposed as an intermediary between mechanical forces and heart development.
source: The NOTCH pathway has been proposed as an intermediary between mechanical forces and heart development [reviewed in Granados-Riveron and Brook (2012)], although the precise mechanotransduction pathway has not been identified.
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature proposing NOTCH as a mechanotransduction pathway in heart development.

claim: Correlations between mechanical forces and NOTCH have been established in adult muscle.
source: In adult muscle, NOTCH signaling has been extensively studied during muscle homeostasis, ageing and regeneration [reviewed in Mourikis and Tajbakhsh (2014)], and correlations between mechanical forces and NOTCH have been established (Carlson et al., 2009; Conboy et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing NOTCH and mechanical forces in adult muscle.

claim: A reduction in the number of satellite cells has been described in adult muscle disuse/unloading animal models.
source: However, a reduction in the number of satellite cells has been described in adult muscle disuse/unloading animal models (Mitchell and Pavlath, 2004; Verdijk et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing satellite cell changes in unloading models.

claim: Training exercises result in an increase of satellite cell number in humans.
source: Conversely, training exercises result in an increase of satellite cell number in humans (Crameri et al., 2004, 2007; Suetta et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing exercise effects on satellite cells in humans.

claim: Physiological exercise increases satellite cell numbers and is beneficial for sarcopenic muscles.
source: Moreover, physiological exercise has been shown to increases satellite cell numbers and to be beneficial for sarcopenic muscles [reviewed in Arthur and Cooley (2012)].
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing exercise benefits for sarcopenic muscles.

claim: Muscle stem cells are sensitive to mechanical forces during muscle development, homeostasis and ageing.
source: Thus, our data and the available information in literature indicate that muscle stem cells are sensitive to mechanical forces during muscle development, homeostasis and ageing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's data and cited literature.

claim: Muscle contraction is necessary to maintain progenitors of the joint in an undifferentiated state and prevents their differentiation into chondrocytes.
source: Muscle contraction is necessary to maintain progenitors of the joint in an undifferentiated state and prevents their differentiation into chondrocytes (Kahn et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing muscle contraction effects on joint progenitors.

claim: Muscle contraction controls chondrocyte convergence extension during cartilage development in zebrafish and mice.
source: Muscle contraction also controls chondrocyte convergence extension during cartilage development in zebrafish and mice (Shwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing muscle contraction effects on cartilage development.

claim: Progenitor cells of the musculoskeletal system are sensitive to mechanical signals generated by muscle contraction during development and respond by several mechanisms.
source: This indicates that progenitor cells of the musculoskeletal system are sensitive to mechanical signals generated by muscle contraction during development and respond to mechanical activity by several mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited literature and the current study.

claim: In plants, physical forces contribute to stem cell maintenance acting on a master regulator (STM homeobox) of Arabidopsis shoot meristems by a mechanism independent of cell proliferation.
source: Interestingly in plants, physical forces contribute to stem cell maintenance acting on a master regulator (STM homeobox) of Arabidopsis shoot meristems, and this is achieved by a mechanism that is independent of cell proliferation (Landrein et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing mechanical forces in plant stem cell maintenance.

claim: Chondrocyte proliferation is reduced in growth plates of long bone in the absence of muscle contraction.
source: Although chondrocyte proliferation is reduced in growth plates of long bone in the absence of muscle contraction (Roddy et al., 2011), skeletogenesis is also affected by proliferation-independent mechanisms after immobilization.
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing chondrocyte proliferation in immobilization.

claim: YAP is upregulated in alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma and is a potent modulator of rhabdomyosarcoma formation.
source: Consistently, YAP is upregulated in alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma and is a potent modulator of rhabdomyosarcoma formation (Crose et al., 2014; Tremblay et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP in rhabdomyosarcoma.

claim: YAP is upregulated in muscle fibers by mechanical overload and is critical for the size of skeletal muscle fibers in adult mice.
source: However, in addition to YAP function in muscle cell proliferation, YAP was recently shown to be upregulated in muscle fibers by mechanical overload and to be critical for the size of skeletal muscle fibers in adult mice (Goodman et al., 2015; Watt et al., 2015), highlighting an additional YAP function in post-mitotic muscle fibers upon loading.
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP function in adult muscle fibers.

claim: YAP and NOTCH pathways have been shown to converge in many biological systems in mice.
source: YAP and NOTCH pathways have been shown to converge in many biological systems in mice (Li et al., 2012, Yimlamai et al., 2014, Manderfield et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature describing YAP-NOTCH pathway convergence.
